vignette:
Tariq was forty years old, a software engineer who had built his life around precision and order. That sense of control was shattered on a Tuesday afternoon when a flash flood tore through his suburban neighborhood. He had been in his home office, the rain a steady drum, when the creek behind his house swelled beyond its banks. He remembered the sound first-a deep, grinding roar that grew into a physical pressure against the walls. Then the water came, brown and fast, climbing the stairs as he scrambled to get his wife and daughter to the attic. He could not sequence the next hours correctly; the images came in fragments-his daughter's scream, the ambulance siren that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere, the paramedic's hand on his shoulder making him flinch. The memories, when they surfaced, were not like normal recollections. They arrived with the full weight of that moment: the smell of wet earth, the cold pressure of the water against his legs, and the sound of that roar repeating in his ears as if it were happening again. He had come to believe that someone else-a better man, a quicker thinker-would not have let his family get trapped like that. Nothing good could happen anymore, he told himself; the happiness he had once felt had been replaced by a constant, grinding misery that colored everything gray.

In the months that followed, Tariq found himself scanning every room he entered for escape routes. At work, in the open-plan office, he always chose a desk near the stairwell. When a colleague touched his shoulder to get his attention, he would jerk away, his heart hammering. The startle response to unexpected movement became a near-daily occurrence-a delivery driver walking past his cubicle, a child running in the park-and each time, the flood memory would surge back, vivid and disorienting. The more he was startled, the more he believed that he was broken, that his capacity for happiness was gone forever. He began to ruminate about the flood itself, not as a natural disaster but as a personal injustice; he caught himself planning how he might get even with the storm, with the county officials who had not warned him, with a world that had let this happen. He forced himself to think only positive thoughts, repeating mantras about gratitude and resilience, but the effort left him exhausted and the misery only deepened. This positive reframing became a ritual-he would stand in his kitchen, hands gripping the counter, reciting affirmations-but it never silenced the roar in his head or the certainty that no good could come. The fact that he still needed to do this every morning, that the ritual never felt optional, told him something he couldn't argue with: that the threat was still there, still waiting, and that without the mantras it would overwhelm him entirely.

The avoidance was subtle at first. He stopped driving past the hospital where the paramedics had taken his family, even though it added twenty minutes to his commute. Each detour confirmed, in a way he never examined, that something dangerous still lurked in that part of town - otherwise, why would his body still insist on avoiding it? He declined his wife's suggestion of a routine physical, saying he was too busy. The sight of an ambulance on the highway would make his hands tremble on the wheel, and he would take the next exit, heart pounding, the memory of that Tuesday flooding back in full sensory detail. Each time he avoided, he told himself it was sensible, but the relief was short-lived. The startle responses grew worse; he began identifying escape routes even in his own home, noting which windows could open, which doors led outside. The threat felt constant, as if danger were a living thing that moved just behind his peripheral vision. And the more vigilant he became, the more the memories intruded, and the more he felt that his old self-the happy, confident man his wife had married-was gone forever.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was not the misery itself, but a moment of quiet terror. His daughter had run up behind him to hug him, and he had spun around, fists raised, before he recognized her face. The look in her eyes-shock, then hurt-was worse than the flood. He called a therapist the next morning. What frightened him most was the possibility that this vigilance, this constant scanning for threat, had become permanent. He was terrified that he would never stop reacting, never stop feeling that the next disaster was already gathering force just out of sight. He hoped, against the weight of his own certainty, that someone could help him find a way back to the man he used to be.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, positive reframing) cause or strengthen negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, positive reframing) cause or increase the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
